{{short description|Integer named after Reo Fortune}}
{{Distinguish|Lucky number}}
{{unsolved|mathematics|Are any Fortunate numbers composite? (Fortune's conjecture)}}
In [[number theory]], a '''Fortunate number''' is the smallest integer <math>m > 1</math> such that, for a given positive [[integer]] <math>n</math>, <math>p_n\#+m</math> is a [[prime number]], where the [[primorial]] <math>p_n\#</math> is the product of the first <math>n</math> prime numbers. They are named after [[Reo Fortune]].

For example, to find the seventh Fortunate number, one would first calculate the product of the first seven primes, which is
:<math>2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17 = 510510.</math>
Adding 2 to that gives another even number, while adding 3 would give another multiple of 3. One would similarly rule out the integers up to 18. Adding 19, however, gives 510529, which is prime. Hence 19 is a Fortunate number. 

The Fortunate numbers for the first primorials are:
:<math>3, 5, 7, 13, 23, 17, 19, 23, 37, 61, 67, 61, 71, 47, 107, 59, 61, 109, 89, 103, 79, 151, 197,\dots</math>
{{OEIS|id=A005235}}. The Fortunate numbers sorted in numerical order with duplicates removed are
:<math>3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 23, 37, 47, 59, 61, 67, 71, 79, 89, 101, 103, 107, 109, 127, 151, 157, 163, 167, 191, 197, \dots</math>
{{OEIS|id=A046066}}.

Fortune conjectured that no Fortunate number is [[Composite number|composite]].{{sfnp|Guy|1994|pp=[https://archive.org/details/unsolvedproblems0000guyr/page/7 7–8]}} A '''Fortunate prime''' is a Fortunate number which is also a prime number. {{As of|2017}}, all known Fortunate numbers are prime, checked up to <math>n=3000</math>.

The Fortunate number for <math>p_n\#</math> is always above <math>p_n</math> and all its divisors are larger than <math>p_n</math>. This is because <math>p_n\#+m</math> is divisible by the [[prime factor]]s of <math>m</math> not larger than <math>p_n</math>. It follows that if a composite Fortunate number does exist, it must be greater than or equal to <math>p_{n+1}^2</math>.<ref name=primepages>{{cite web | url=https://t5k.org/glossary/page.php?sort=FortunateNumber | title=Prime Glossary: Fortunate number | website=PrimePages | access-date=24 August 2026}}</ref>

Paul Carpenter defines the '''less Fortunate numbers''' as the differences between <math>p_n\#</math> and the largest prime less than <math>p_n\# - 1</math>. These are also conjectured to be always prime.<ref name=primepages/>
